article_title: The Essential Playbook for Family Engagement in Middle School
citation: Wallace, M., & Paredes, M. (2024). The essential playbook for family engagement in middle school. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Monitor, evaluate, and share engagement outcomes to drive continuous improvement
description: The Outcomes element treats measurable indicators as the basis for assessing engagement efforts: "Make data-driven decisions to align improvements with school growth." Schools collect and evaluate feedback data, share findings openly with staff, families, and community partners to promote transparency and trust, and use results to refine plans in a cycle of continuous improvement.
requirements: A data collection plan and tools, such as surveys of teachers, families, and students, family focus groups, exit tickets, and student attendance records
target_learners: middle school students and their families
target_learning_goals: verifying that engagement efforts meet intended objectives and improving them over time
examples: Illustrative Table 4 lists surveys, family focus groups, exit tickets after professional development and family activities, and attendance records as measurement tools
key_sources: Wallace, M., & Paredes, M. (2024). The essential playbook for family engagement in middle school. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED663740

article_title: Systems Alignment and Coherence: Opportunities for Alameda County's Early Care and Education System
citation: Walrond, N., Serwanga, R., & Farrell, G. (2025). Systems alignment and coherence: Opportunities for Alameda County's early care and education system. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Share early care information through trusted community channels and in families' routine settings and languages
description: The report presents strategic communication as both an engine and a by-product of alignment and coherence, and recommends bidirectional communication that builds awareness while gathering timely, honest feedback. Listening session participants "asked for materials to be shared in places that are part of their routines (such as faith communities or community resource centers)," translated into multiple languages, and delivered through trusted community leaders. The principle holds that outreach should meet families where they are.
requirements: Communication channels that are diverse and fully accessible to meet language, technology, and diverse ability needs
constraints: The report notes some communities, such as the Mam community, rely on word-of-mouth information sharing, requiring tailored channels
target_learners: Families with young children in Oakland and Alameda County, including communities that are often marginalized and harder to reach
target_learning_goals: Awareness of and access to high-quality early care and learning opportunities
examples: First 5 Alameda invests in trusted relationships through programs for providers (Quality Counts), families (Help Me Grow), the public (AlamedaKids.org), and policymakers (board of supervisors district data profiles)
key_sources: Walrond, N., Serwanga, R., & Farrell, G. (2025). Systems alignment and coherence: Opportunities for Alameda County's early care and education system. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673491

article_title: The Arc of Dual Enrollment: Access, Struggle, and What Makes Success Possible
citation: Terrell, J. H., Mathias, J., Blanchard, A., & Roldan-Rueda, D. (2026). The arc of dual enrollment: Access, struggle, and what makes success possible. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: OUSD open-access dual enrollment support model with the Point Person role
description: Oakland Unified School District's support model for open-access dual enrollment centers on the Point Person: "a designated K–12 staff member in each dual enrollment classroom whose explicit role is to stay in proactive contact with dual enrollment students throughout the semester, track progress in coordination with both high school and college instructors, and reach out before small difficulties become insurmountable ones." It is paired with school-day academic support, navigation assistance, and professional development, and the program reports an average pass rate of 83 percent, reaching 90 to 91 percent in recent semesters.
requirements: Investment in proactive outreach staffing, integrated academic support, navigation assistance, and instructor professional development
constraints: The model is described in a companion case study (Terrell et al., 2026b); this brief reports it as a single-district example without causal evaluation
target_learners: High school students across a wide range of academic backgrounds, including many from low-income and first-generation backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Passing dual enrollment courses and navigating college systems and expectations
examples: OUSD achieved an average pass rate of 83 percent across the program while maintaining open access, with recent semesters reaching 90 to 91 percent
key_sources: Terrell, J. H., Mathias, J., Blanchard, A., & Roldan-Rueda, D. (2026). The arc of dual enrollment: Access, struggle, and what makes success possible. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED681344

article_title: Preparing Students for AI-Powered Materials Discovery: A Workflow-Aligned Framework for AI Literacy, Equity, and Scientific Judgment
citation: Dongming Mei, Katherine Moore, and Ben Sayler. (2026). Preparing Students for AI-Powered Materials Discovery: A Workflow-Aligned Framework for AI Literacy, Equity, and Scientific Judgment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09624
title: Outcome-oriented equity framework distinguishing access equity from impact equity
description: The paper distinguishes access equity, whether students and institutions can obtain devices, broadband, software, and support, from impact equity, whether AI-enabled learning produces comparable gains across subgroups. It argues that 'Access without learning gains can reproduce inequality in a more technologically sophisticated form, while learning gains observed only in average outcomes can obscure subgroup harms.' Evaluation should use disaggregated evidence on learning gains, transfer, persistence, and confidence calibration.
requirements: Subgroup analyses should be conducted only when data can be collected ethically, sample sizes are sufficient, and privacy protections are in place
constraints: The paper notes subgroup-sensitive evaluation is methodologically demanding due to small samples, missing demographic data, and privacy constraints
target_learners: students across subgroups including rural students, English learners, first-generation students, and students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: comparable conceptual understanding, transfer of learning, confidence calibration, persistence, and research readiness across subgroups
examples: The paper recommends metrics including differential learning gains between subgroups, transfer to unfamiliar tasks, and confidence calibration across demographics, institutions, rurality, and prior-preparation levels
key_sources: Dongming Mei, Katherine Moore, and Ben Sayler. (2026). Preparing Students for AI-Powered Materials Discovery: A Workflow-Aligned Framework for AI Literacy, Equity, and Scientific Judgment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09624

article_title: Evaluation in the Age of AI: Output as Evidence of Learning
citation: Md Zarzees Uddin Shah Chowdhury and Samin Rahman Khan. (2026). Evaluation in the Age of AI: Output as Evidence of Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22660
title: The output-as-evidence model and its collapse: generative AI decouples produced artifacts from the cognitive labor they were meant to certify
description: The article's organizing framework is the 'output-as-evidence' model: the assumption that a student artifact (essay, proof, code) is a direct reflection of cognitive labor, resting on "the assumption of proportional effort". Generative AI collapses the novice-expert production barrier, so the final product no longer signals that mental processes occurred, creating a verification problem existing institutions cannot resolve. The authors call this the proxy crisis and argue the focus on 'cheating' misses a structural misalignment between assessment design and learning outcomes.
requirements: Assessment regimes must treat artifacts as proxies for cognitive processes, which requires that attribution of the artifact to a specific cognitive agent be reliable
constraints: The authors state no surface-level task modification (specificity, realism, multimodal components) reliably distinguishes AI-generated from human-generated responses without rethinking what is assessed
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: genuine understanding, reasoning, and judgment as demonstrated through assessment
examples: The article cites Deans et al.'s comparative analysis in which ChatGPT-generated graduate coursework performed at or above passing levels and even domain experts detected it only marginally better than chance.
key_sources: Md Zarzees Uddin Shah Chowdhury and Samin Rahman Khan. (2026). Evaluation in the Age of AI: Output as Evidence of Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22660

article_title: From Student Risk Prediction to SC2R: Semantics-Constrained Counterfactual Recourse for Educational Decision Support
citation: Ngoc Luyen Le, Marie-Hélène Abel, Bertrand Laforge. (2026). From Student Risk Prediction to SC2R: Semantics-Constrained Counterfactual Recourse for Educational Decision Support. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17618
title: OULAD snapshot evaluation protocol with leakage-excluded presentation-level split
description: The evaluation protocol constructs two snapshots per eligible student per assessment, at t = d-14 and t = d-7 before the due day, using only information available up to snapshot time; post-t interactions and assessments are excluded. Features include "aggregated click counts by activity type over rolling 7-, 14-, and 28-day windows", availability-alignment features, prior assessment history, time-to-deadline variables, and immutable learner descriptors. Data are split at the module-presentation level (15 train, 2 validation, 5 test presentations) to avoid leakage across closely related offerings, with pass defined as score >= 40.
requirements: Snapshots must exclude post-t information to avoid leakage
Splits at module-presentation level to avoid leakage across related offerings
constraints: Early assessments that would induce negative snapshot times are handled during preprocessing
target_learners: Open University students in the OULAD dataset
target_learning_goals: next-assessment pass/fail prediction and recourse generation
examples: Table II reports 190,752 train, 29,054 validation, and 84,791 test instances per horizon, with d-14 as the main horizon and d-7 as secondary
key_sources: Ngoc Luyen Le, Marie-Hélène Abel, Bertrand Laforge. (2026). From Student Risk Prediction to SC2R: Semantics-Constrained Counterfactual Recourse for Educational Decision Support. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17618

article_title: Artificial intelligence in vocational education and training: A systematic review of educational purposes, theoretical conceptualizations, and empirical effectiveness
citation: Deutscher, V., Thomann, H., Zlatkin-Troitschanskaia, O., Weyland, U., Abele, S., Danek, A. H., Greiff, S., Rausch, A., Seeber, S., Seifried, J., & Winther, E. (2026). Artificial intelligence in vocational education and training: A systematic review of educational purposes, theoretical conceptualizations, and empirical effectiveness. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence 11 (2026) 100628. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100628
title: Three paradigms of AI integration in education: AI-directed learner-as-receiver, AI-supported learner-as-collaborator, AI-empowered learner-as-leader
description: The review adopts Ouyang and Jiao's (2021) framework, which "frames the educational role of AI along three paradigms that reflect increasing levels of learner agency": AI-directed (learner-as-receiver, rooted in behaviorism, with AI structuring content and giving prescriptive feedback), AI-supported (learner-as-collaborator, grounded in cognitive and social constructivist theories, with dialogic tutoring and exploratory environments), and AI-empowered (learner-as-leader, aligned with connectivism and complex adaptive systems theory, where learners co-design learning trajectories). The review uses this framework as the coding scheme for RQ3 on theoretical conceptualization of human–AI interaction.
requirements: The framework is used to code each study's theoretical grounding and AI's role in learner interaction, requiring classification of pedagogical foundations, technological manifestations, and the human–AI interface.
constraints: The review notes that in the AI-supported paradigm the learning space and learning goals are mostly predefined, and that the reviewed VET studies concentrate in the AI-directed paradigm.
target_learners: vocational education and training learners
target_learning_goals: characterizing the pedagogical role of AI in learning environments
examples: The review coded all 26 included studies against this framework, finding most applications in the AI-directed paradigm with traditional intelligent tutoring systems as prototypes.
key_sources: Deutscher, V., Thomann, H., Zlatkin-Troitschanskaia, O., Weyland, U., Abele, S., Danek, A. H., Greiff, S., Rausch, A., Seeber, S., Seifried, J., & Winther, E. (2026). Artificial intelligence in vocational education and training: A systematic review of educational purposes, theoretical conceptualizations, and empirical effectiveness. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence 11 (2026) 100628. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100628

article_title: Synthesizing frameworks of higher education student learning outcomes
citation: Markle, R., Brenneman, M., Jackson, T., Burrus, J., & Robbins, S. (2013). Synthesizing Frameworks of Higher Education Student Learning Outcomes. ETS Research Report Series, ETS RR-13-22. http://search.ets.org/researcher
title: Distinguish terminal higher education outcomes from underlying workforce skills when designing frameworks and assessments
description: The report argues that frameworks defining what a student should have achieved in college differ from those certifying workforce competencies. "By definition, an outcome is a terminal point and not an underlying skill or ability"; outcome demonstrations involve complex applications and interactions of basic skills, whereas measuring individual underlying traits may be more valuable for identifying those likely to succeed at work, for reasons including ease of assessment and more direct observation.
requirements: Framework designers must decide whether the target is a terminal demonstrated outcome of education or an underlying skill or trait predictive of workplace success
constraints: The distinction is articulated for comparing higher education outcome frameworks with workforce competency models; the report does not claim one approach is universally superior
target_learners: higher education students and graduates entering the workforce
examples: The report contrasts the National Work Readiness Certificate, which uses work-contextualized cognitive test items, with educationally focused frameworks such as the DQP and LEAP
key_sources: Markle, R., Brenneman, M., Jackson, T., Burrus, J., & Robbins, S. (2013). Synthesizing Frameworks of Higher Education Student Learning Outcomes. ETS Research Report Series, ETS RR-13-22. http://search.ets.org/researcher

article_title: Sixth-grade students’ reasoning on the order relation of integers as influenced by prior experience: an inferentialist analysis
citation: Maike Schindler, Stephan Hußmann, Per Nilsson, Arthur Bakker. (2017). Sixth-grade students' reasoning on the order relation of integers as influenced by prior experience: an inferentialist analysis. Math Ed Res J 29:471–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13394-017-0202-x
title: 'Out of the Debts' learning environment combining the debts-and-assets context with the number line
description: A learning environment developed by Hußmann and Schindler (2014a, b) in the KOSIMA project, which aims at teaching mathematics through real contexts. Students play a board game in groups of four in which each is an indebted person aiming to redeem debts; the board is a number line ('account bar') with positive and negative numbers, and players draw changing account balances with their pieces. Later problems invite reflection on positions on the account bar and the role of the minus sign, with temperatures and altitudes as further contexts.
requirements: Students should be involved in the GoGAR, drawing on out-of-school experiences and inferentially relating their reasoning to external representations
target_learners: sixth-grade students in German secondary school
target_learning_goals: understanding negative integers and the order relation
examples: In the study, students reflected on the context, e.g. on the possession of too many luxury goods ('I do not really need a car!')
key_sources: Maike Schindler, Stephan Hußmann, Per Nilsson, Arthur Bakker. (2017). Sixth-grade students' reasoning on the order relation of integers as influenced by prior experience: an inferentialist analysis. Math Ed Res J 29:471–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13394-017-0202-x

article_title: When failure fails to be productive: probing the effectiveness of productive failure for learning beyond STEM domains
citation: Valentina Nachtigall · Katja Serova · Nikol Rummel. (2020). When failure fails to be productive: probing the effectiveness of productive failure for learning beyond STEM domains. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09525-2
title: Out-of-school lab for social sciences as a setting for PF-based learning of research methods
description: The studies took place in an interdisciplinary out-of-school lab at a large German university, offering projects for secondary students. The article describes that "Out-of-school labs are non-formal learning settings that are assumed to be highly authentic environments for learning scientific ways of thinking and working due to their location\
examples: PF students role-played educational researchers designing a study to investigate teachers' and parents' suggestions about improving teaching, within the lab-based teacher-conference scenario.

article_title: A large-scale implementation of predictive learning analytics in higher education: the teachers’ role and perspective
citation: Herodotou, C., Rienties, B., Boroowa, A., Zdrahal, Z., & Hlosta, M. (2019). A large-scale implementation of predictive learning analytics in higher education: the teachers' role and perspective. Education Tech Research Dev, 67, 1273–1306. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09685-0
title: OU Analyse (OUA) predictive learning analytics system and dashboard
description: OUA is a PLA system built at the Open University UK that "uses a range of advanced statistical and machine learning approaches to predict students at-risk so that cost-effective interventions can be made." It combines four predictive models (Naïve Bayes, CART, k-NN with demographic data, k-NN with VLE data) via voting to predict whether students will submit their next teacher-marked assessment and complete the course. Teachers access predictions through a dashboard showing cohort comparisons, per-student predictions, and nearest-neighbour views; contact with students happens outside the dashboard.
requirements: Machine learning models are trained on legacy data from the previous presentation of the same course
Weekly VLE interaction data and student demographics must be recorded and available
constraints: Predictions target only students who have not yet submitted the next TMA
Accuracy is relatively stable across presentations but increases toward the end of a course presentation
target_learners: distance learning higher education students in Level 1 undergraduate courses
examples: Predictions are computed weekly from static (demographic) and behavioural (VLE activity types such as forum, content, resource, glossary, wiki) data, with precision, recall, F-measure and accuracy tracked per week (Fig. 1)
key_sources: Herodotou, C., Rienties, B., Boroowa, A., Zdrahal, Z., & Hlosta, M. (2019). A large-scale implementation of predictive learning analytics in higher education: the teachers' role and perspective. Education Tech Research Dev, 67, 1273–1306. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09685-0

article_title: Exploring expert perceptions of creativity in instructional design: a phenomenographic study
citation: Carolina Cuesta-Hincapie. (2025). Exploring expert perceptions of creativity in instructional design: a phenomenographic study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10560-4
title: Outcome space of expert ways of experiencing creativity in ID: two dimensions with progression from understanding creativity to perceiving pedagogical challenge
description: The article's organizing framework is an outcome space in which the four categories of description form a progression from less to more comprehensive ways of experiencing creativity in ID. The article states the "outcome space was two-dimensional", with one dimension covering how participants understood and enacted creativity and one covering how they perceive creativity in the ID field. Progression from Category 1 to Category 4 "represents increasingly comprehensive ways of experiencing and conceptualizing creativity in ID".
requirements: Categories must be generated from collective participant experience rather than individual meaning, per the phenomenographic method the article follows
constraints: Derived from six purposefully selected experts; the article presents the categories as relative, experiential, and context-orientated rather than judging their accuracy
target_learners: instructional design graduate students and educators
target_learning_goals: understanding and fostering creativity in instructional design practice and education
examples: Category 1: creativity is a skill requiring intentionality; Category 2: creativity is fundamental in ID but not acknowledged; Category 3: creativity relates to the designer's character; Category 4: creativity as a pedagogical challenge in ID education
key_sources: Carolina Cuesta-Hincapie. (2025). Exploring expert perceptions of creativity in instructional design: a phenomenographic study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10560-4

article_title: Learning Outcomes, Assessment, and Evaluation in Educational Recommender Systems: A Systematic Review
citation: Nursultan Askarbekuly, Ivan Luković. (2024). Learning Outcomes, Assessment, and Evaluation in Educational Recommender Systems: A Systematic Review. https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.09500
title: Outcome-based approach: ERS evaluation should be rooted in the achievement of intended learning outcomes
description: The review adopts an outcome-based approach in which learning is defined through the achievement of intended learning outcomes, and argues that "the evaluation of educational recommender systems should be rooted in outcome-based assessment". Under this approach, target metrics should be learning-centered and derived from learning outcomes, and systems should verify that intended outcomes are achieved through assessment. The authors state that in their earlier works they demonstrated it is possible to align intended outcomes, learning activities, and learning assessment when building an educational product.
requirements: Intended learning outcomes must be defined for the learner, and assessment activities aligned with those outcomes, as in constructive alignment
constraints: The review acknowledges the outcome-oriented approach is not always applicable, for example in the affective learning domain where outcomes are open-ended rather than pre-defined
target_learners: learners in formal and informal e-learning settings
examples: The review evaluates existing ERS research against this approach, checking what metrics systems optimize and how they verify outcome achievement
key_sources: Nursultan Askarbekuly, Ivan Luković. (2024). Learning Outcomes, Assessment, and Evaluation in Educational Recommender Systems: A Systematic Review. https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.09500

article_title: Output-Based Instruction, Learning Styles and Vocabulary Learning in the EFL Context of Iran
citation: Behnaz Rastegar & Fatemeh Safari. (2017). Output-Based Instruction, Learning Styles and Vocabulary Learning in the EFL Context of Iran. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 5(2). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.5n.2p.101
title: Swain's output hypothesis and structured output-based vocabulary tasks
description: The article grounds its intervention in Swain's output hypothesis (1985), which "posits that production of language has a direct effect on acquisition of language by language learners," operating through three functions: noticing/triggering, hypothesis testing, and metalinguistic function. Tasks were designed using Lee and VanPatten's (2003) concept of structured output-based tasks, whose features include "presenting things one by one," meaning-focused activities, connecting sentences, using both output modes, collaborative responding, and sufficient knowledge of form. The study operationalized this as pushing learners to produce sentences with target words orally or in writing.
requirements: Output should be presented in a structured manner, following Lee and VanPatten's features of structured output
Learners must produce language themselves rather than receive only teacher-provided examples
constraints: The article's empirical support comes from a single quasi-experimental study at one Iranian language institute with intermediate learners
target_learners: Intermediate EFL learners
examples: In the oral groups, words were presented and practiced orally with pronunciation feedback and peer negotiation of meaning; in the written groups, learners copied words, wrote sentences, and received teacher corrections at the end of each session
key_sources: Behnaz Rastegar & Fatemeh Safari. (2017). Output-Based Instruction, Learning Styles and Vocabulary Learning in the EFL Context of Iran. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 5(2). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.5n.2p.101

article_title: Output-Based Instruction, Learning Styles and Vocabulary Learning in the EFL Context of Iran
citation: Behnaz Rastegar & Fatemeh Safari. (2017). Output-Based Instruction, Learning Styles and Vocabulary Learning in the EFL Context of Iran. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 5(2). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.5n.2p.101
title: Use oral or written output-based instruction as an alternative when input-based vocabulary teaching fails
description: The article recommends output-oriented teaching procedures, in which learners produce language themselves, as an alternative to input-based instruction to "enhance learners’ understanding and practice opportunities." Teachers are advised to adopt output-based instruction "in situations where input-based teaching fails" and when moving toward learner-based approaches, since producing sentences gives learners more practice and can raise self-confidence.
requirements: Learners must be pushed to produce their own oral or written sentences using target words, with the teacher refraining from producing examples for them
constraints: The supporting evidence comes from one quasi-experimental study of intermediate Iranian EFL learners; oral and written modes did not differ significantly, so either mode may be used
target_learners: Intermediate EFL learners
Adult language learners
target_learning_goals: Vocabulary knowledge in a foreign language
examples: Over 15 sessions, experimental groups produced sentences with target words orally or in writing while the control group received mechanical drills; both experimental conditions outperformed the control on a 30-item posttest
key_sources: Behnaz Rastegar & Fatemeh Safari. (2017). Output-Based Instruction, Learning Styles and Vocabulary Learning in the EFL Context of Iran. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 5(2). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.5n.2p.101

article_title: Does Outdoor Education Make Any Difference in Environmental Literacy of Pre-Service Classroom Teachers?
citation: Aysegul Derman, Elvan Sahin, Esme Hacieminoglu. (2016). Does Outdoor Education Make any Difference in Environmental Literacy of Pre-service Classroom Teachers? INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENVIRONMENTAL & SCIENCE EDUCATION, 11(15), 8491-8506. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
title: 16-week outdoor education program for pre-service classroom teachers
description: A semester-long (16 weeks) environmental education implementation in which pre-service classroom teachers worked in 12 small groups on assigned environmental issues, formulated research questions, searched scientific resources, and shared findings with the lecturer acting as moderator. The program combined indoor active learning with "activities suitable for th e outdoor education model", including field trips to a Bald Ibis reproduction station and Old Halfeti, brainstorming discussions after trips, school visits, and learning "how to plant trees, observe birds, and walk in the open air".
requirements: Groups assigned environmental issues from the curriculum and a lecturer acting as moderator and participant observer throughout the semester
constraints: The study is limited with the classroom pre-service teachers in the experimental and the control groups
target_learners: sophomore classroom pre-service teachers
examples: Field trips to the Bald Ibis reproduction station in Sanlıurfa-Birecik and to Old Halfeti, with post-trip brain-storming discussion; regular visits to primary-school classroom teachers
key_sources: Aysegul Derman, Elvan Sahin, Esme Hacieminoglu. (2016). Does Outdoor Education Make any Difference in Environmental Literacy of Pre-service Classroom Teachers? INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENVIRONMENTAL & SCIENCE EDUCATION, 11(15), 8491-8506. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

article_title: Does Outdoor Education Make Any Difference in Environmental Literacy of Pre-Service Classroom Teachers?
citation: Aysegul Derman, Elvan Sahin, Esme Hacieminoglu. (2016). Does Outdoor Education Make any Difference in Environmental Literacy of Pre-service Classroom Teachers? INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENVIRONMENTAL & SCIENCE EDUCATION, 11(15), 8491-8506. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
title: Use outdoor education with active, student-centered methods to improve pre-service teachers' environmental literacy
description: The article concludes that the outdoor education approach, in which learners actively investigate environmental issues, interact with nature through field trips and outdoor activities, and reflect through discussion, is an effective way to raise pre-service classroom teachers' environmental literacy. It reports that "the outdoor education approach could be used as an effective way in improving the environmental literacy levels of the classroom pre-service teachers", with gains in attitudes and uses and richer qualitative outcomes than lecturing.
requirements: Opportunities for learners to interact with nature and be actively involved in the learning process, with lecturer moderation and group investigation of curriculum environmental issues
constraints: Findings are limited to classroom pre-service teachers in the two studied groups; no significant gains appeared for knowledge or within-group concern
target_learners: pre-service classroom teachers
teacher candidates in higher education
examples: The experimental group's 16-week program combining group research, documentaries, field trips, brainstorming discussions, school visits, tree planting, bird observation and nature walks
key_sources: Aysegul Derman, Elvan Sahin, Esme Hacieminoglu. (2016). Does Outdoor Education Make any Difference in Environmental Literacy of Pre-service Classroom Teachers? INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENVIRONMENTAL & SCIENCE EDUCATION, 11(15), 8491-8506. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

article_title: AI System Usability and Learning Engagement in Nursing Simulation: Cross-Sectional Statistical Indirect Associations Through Extraneous Cognitive Load and Flow Experience.
citation: Liu Mengjiao, Zhang Ping, Wu Yeqing, Pan Lu, Li Lan. (2026). AI System Usability and Learning Engagement in Nursing Simulation: Cross‐Sectional Statistical Indirect Associations Through Extraneous Cognitive Load and Flow Experience. Nursing Open, 13(9): e70855. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70855
title: Beijing Oubeier adaptive nursing virtual simulation platform (Version 3.2)
description: The studied system is a nursing virtual simulation platform developed by Beijing Oubeier Software Technology Development Co. Ltd., comprising the Comprehensive Training System for Basic Nursing Skills and the Critical Care Virtual Simulation System. Version 3.2 (launched 2024) included "more than 50 nursing‐skill modules, with each simulation task typically requiring 20–30 min". It supports multi-terminal access, records operational steps and decision pathways, triggers branch-specific feedback, recommends repeated practice, and adjusts scenario difficulty within preset module structures. The authors emphasize that its adaptive function was rule-based rather than generative AI, so the platform is described as an adaptive virtual simulation system rather than an artificial intelligence or machine-learning system.
requirements: Individual student accounts for multi-terminal access
Use within nursing courses such as Fundamentals of Nursing and Medical-Surgical Nursing
constraints: The adaptive function is rule-based, using prespecified procedural rules, decision branches, and performance thresholds rather than a generative AI model or autonomous model updating
target_learners: Nursing students in associate degree, undergraduate, and postgraduate programmes
target_learning_goals: Nursing assessment, clinical decision-making, and intervention implementation skills in simulation scenarios
examples: Students completed scenario-based tasks involving nursing assessment, clinical decision-making, and intervention implementation, primarily for post-class independent practice
key_sources: Liu Mengjiao, Zhang Ping, Wu Yeqing, Pan Lu, Li Lan. (2026). AI System Usability and Learning Engagement in Nursing Simulation: Cross‐Sectional Statistical Indirect Associations Through Extraneous Cognitive Load and Flow Experience. Nursing Open, 13(9): e70855. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70855

article_title: Dental students' attitudes toward community service: a pre-post survey study of a service-learning experience in Chile.
citation: Leiva Hernández Carolina, Aguilera Felipe Rodrigo, Aravena-Castillo Verónica, Hidalgo V. Viviana, Farías Orellana Javier, Stuardo-Parada Adriana. (2026). Dental students’ attitudes toward community service: a pre–post survey study of a service-learning experience in Chile. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10109-w
title: Service-learning program combining outreach and clinical components over 15 weeks
description: The intervention comprised two complementary components: an outreach component at external organizations (preschools and an elderly care center) delivering oral health promotion and preventive education, and a clinical component at the university providing examination and treatment matched to each population. "Activities took place over 15 weeks, with two weekly sessions of approximately three hours each, allocating an equivalent amount of time to the outreach and clinical components." The program aimed to foster social responsibility, empathy, and understanding of community health needs.
requirements: Institutional community engagement program coordination, including student transportation to external sites
Balance between service and learning with curricular integration and structured reflection

title: Obstetric Ultrasound Competency Assessment Tool (OUCAT)

title: Obstetric Ultrasound Competency Assessment Tool (OUCAT) with 45-point pass/fail and 70-point mastery learning standards
description: OUCAT is "a validated checklist" used to quantify residents' obstetric ultrasound skill levels on the simulator, with scoring videos rated by two blinded consultants and the average taken as the final score. Pass/fail standards were set by the contrast group method using expert data from 24 certified obstetric ultrasound experts: "45 points was taken as the pass/fail score, and mastery learning level was established at 70 points". Mastery levels were defined for the overall examination and each task module.
requirements: Validity evidence collected against expert performance; assessments performed on simulators within 30 minutes; evaluation videos scored by two consultants with participant identities and test status blinded
constraints: Assessment focused on basic operational skills using a normal fetal module; pass/fail cutoff set to minimize passing inexperienced trainees and failing experts
target_learners: Obstetric ultrasound residents at varying experience levels
examples: Expert assessment data were used to establish pass/fail and mastery learning levels in a prior multi-center validity study by the same team

article_title: Framing Metrics, Outcomes, and Assessment Overview in Leadership Programs.
citation: Hastings, L. J., and D. Rosch. 2025. "Framing Metrics, Outcomes, and Assessment Overview in Leadership Programs." New Directions for Student Leadership 2025, no. 187: 85–91. https://doi.org/10.1002/yd.70007
title: Outcomes-assessment-metrics alignment framework for leadership program evaluation
description: The article presents metrics, outcomes, and assessment as an interrelated system for leadership program evaluation: stated outcomes drive the assessment plan, and metrics execute that plan. The authors state that "Stated program outcomes ultimately drive the plan for assessment, and its metrics are the mechanism through which the assessment plan is successfully executed," with outcomes foreshadowing metrics and metrics mapped to the assessment plan.
requirements: Program outcomes must be articulated first and in a way that foreshadows the metric through which they will be assessed, with metrics mapped to the assessment plan and the plan mapped to outcomes
target_learners: college and university students in leadership education programs
target_learning_goals: leadership learning and leader development outcomes

title: 'Our Care Through Our Eyes' co-designed self-harm e-learning programme (three 15-minute RLO packages)
description: A digital education intervention made of reusable learning objects — digital resources with a single learning objective engaging users in four learning components — co-designed by children and young people, registered children's nurses and academics. It consists of three short (15 min) e-learning packages covering understanding self-harm and care pathways, effective communication with CYP following self-harm admission, and assessing risk and managing safety. This study evaluated it in a new hospital setting with new outcome measures.
requirements: Delivered via e-learning to registered children's nurses caring for CYP admitted after self-harm
constraints: Evaluated only in a single site; the article notes it is difficult to generalize to other registered children's nurses
target_learners: Registered children's nurses in acute paediatric inpatient settings
target_learning_goals: Effective communication with CYP after self-harm admission
examples: Participants valued printable conversation techniques and videos showing real conversations CYP found helpful or unhelpful

title: 'Our Care through Our Eyes' co-produced digital educational intervention (three reusable learning objects)
description: A digital educational programme hosted on an online platform, composed of reusable learning objects co-produced with CYP service users, registered children's nurses and academics. RLOs are "short, self-contained, focused 'chunks' of e-learning underpinned by learning theory comprising multimedia rich content, activities and self-assessment". The final intervention consisted of three RLOs covering understanding self-harm and care pathways, effective communication, and assessing risk and managing safety, delivered through multimedia including videos of youth actors narrating CYP experiences. It was piloted with seven student nurses to test functionality, face validity and time requirement, and evaluated in the uncontrolled pre–post study.
requirements: Co-production with service users, professionals and academics using a validated RLO development methodology with specification and review tools for each stage of the process
constraints: Content is specific to caring for CYP admitted with self-harm in acute paediatric inpatient care; evidence-based and expert peer-reviewed content varied across the three RLOs
target_learners: Registered children's nurses providing acute care in paediatric settings
target_learning_goals: Effective communication with CYP following self-harm admission
Assessing risk and managing safety with CYP admitted with self-harm
examples: Piloted with seven student nurses (child field) to test functionality, face validity and time requirement; functioned on Macintosh and Windows platforms and PC, iPad, iPhone and Android devices
